meta.title: Who really said "We can easily forgive a child who is afraid of the dark; the real tragedy of life is when men are afraid of the light"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No — Plato never wrote this. It appears in none of his dialogues and in no published work until recent years. A modern feel-good line wrongly pinned on Plato.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'We can easily forgive a child who is afraid of the dark; the real tragedy of life is when men are afraid of the light'?
meta.ogDescription: Plato never wrote this. It appears in none of his works and in no book until recent years — a modern paraphrase misattributed to Plato.

answer.label: Not Plato — a modern misattribution
answer.sourceLine: This polished line appears in none of Plato’s dialogues or letters. Per Wikiquote’s Misattributed section ↗, it “cannot be found in any of Plato’s writings, nor … in any published work anywhere until recent years” — the hallmark of a modern feel-good line pinned on a famous ancient name. No documented author for the exact wording has been found.

source.heading: What the record shows

docMeta.dd: Not found in any dialogue or letter
Modern web era; absent from published books until recent years

source.excerpt: We can easily forgive a child who is afraid of the dark; the real tragedy of life is when men are afraid of the light.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ lists the line under Misattributed: it “cannot be found in any of Plato’s writings, nor … in any published work anywhere until recent years.”
Researcher Ian Chadwick, after checking hundreds of sites, found no credible source ↗ tying it to Plato, calling it “another bloody stupid Internet meme.”
The nearest real ancient thought is Lucretius ↗ (II.55–61): children fear everything in the dark, “so we in the light sometimes fear” things no more real — a different point, and not Plato.
Quote aggregators such as Goodreads ↗ and BrainyQuote credit Plato with no citation, which is how the misattribution spread.
source.excerptNote: Widely circulated as Plato — but traceable to no work of his, and to no published source before the internet age.
source.rightsNote: Because the exact wording traces to no identifiable author or first-publication, no copyright status can be honestly asserted. The genuine ancient antecedent — Lucretius’ De Rerum Natura (1st century BC) — is in the public domain in its original Latin, but that is a different sentence, and modern English translations of Lucretius may themselves be in copyright.

author.name: Plato
author.heading: About the misattributed name
author.metaLine: c. 428–348 BC · Athenian philosopher, student of Socrates, teacher of Aristotle
author.bio: Plato founded the Academy in Athens and wrote in dialogue form, most famously the Republic with its Allegory of the Cave — prisoners who mistake shadows for reality and are dazzled when turned toward the light. That vivid dark-and-light imagery is almost certainly why this modern aphorism gets slapped onto his name, but the sentence itself matches nothing in his surviving corpus.

cite.sourceCitation: No primary source; earliest documented only as an uncited internet-era attribution to Plato. Nearest genuine antecedent: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura, Book II, lines 55–61, trans. W. H. D. Rouse (Loeb Classical Library).

misattribution.heading: How a modern line became “Plato”
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook feel-good misquote: a clever, uplifting sentence attached to one of history’s most quotable names with no source behind it.

items.why: The sentence is absent from every Platonic dialogue and letter. Wikiquote ↗ files it as misattributed, noting it appears in no published work until recent years — almost certainly borrowed credibility from Plato’s Allegory of the Cave.

Writer Ian Chadwick speculated the line “feels far more modern than anything Plato ever wrote” and might trace to Robin Sharma’s self-help writing, but could not confirm it ↗. Treat this as a hunch, not an attribution.

items.scope: A real but different ancient thought
items.why: Some trace the sentiment to Lucretius’ line ↗ that we fear in daylight as children fear the dark — but that says the opposite of “afraid of the light” and is neither Plato nor the quoted wording.

misattribution.truthLine: Verdict: not Plato. The exact sentence has no documented source and appears in no book before the internet age — a modern aphorism riding on Plato’s name, per Wikiquote ↗.

context.heading: Why it sticks to Plato
lead: Plato’s Republic gave the world its most famous parable of illumination: prisoners chained in a cave who take flickering shadows for reality, and who are blinded — even hostile — when dragged up into the sunlight. A pithy line about grown men being “afraid of the light” slots so neatly into that imagery that few readers pause to ask whether Plato actually wrote it.
He didn’t. The value of tracing these lines is not to deny the thought its charm but to separate a genuine 2,400-year-old text from a modern sentence wearing an ancient mask.
context.pull: It fits the Allegory of the Cave so well that no one checks — which is exactly how misquotes survive.
